newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Future Lithuania PM sees 1998 end to litas peg.
newsitem.headline: Future Lithuania PM sees 1998 end to litas peg.

text.p: Lithuania's prime minister-designate Gediminas Vagnorius on Monday said he foresaw an end to the peg of the country's litas currency to the dollar in around 18 months, after presidential elections are held.
Vagnorius, named as future premier after a first round of parliamentary elections in October, has pushed to allow the litas to float freely and end its four-to-one peg to the dollar.

Vagnorius' Homeland Union party strengthened its position in a second round of elections on Sunday, getting a total of 70 seats in parliament out of 141, preliminary figures showed on Monday. Presidential elections are due in February 1998.
The litas' rate is regulated under a currency board system, under which the central bank has to have enough reserves in its vaults to match the currency in circulation.
But the central bank is also deprived of any powers to manage monetary policy or the exchange rate under the system.
"The most probable situation is that we will see a free exchange rate and a departure from the currency board in 18 months," Vagnorius told Reuters on Monday.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) strongly backs keeping the currency board, as it says it has helped bring down inflation and create trust in the litas.
The currency board is part of Lithuania's agreements with the IMF and has to stay in place under these accords until September 1997.

Some foreign investors have been worried that Vagnorius' plans mean a devaluation of the litas but the future prime minister said he did not want panic and reiterated he was against a devaluation of the currency.

He said there would be a gradual shift in the currency system, starting from January 1997 when the central bank would start to take on more powers, including the right to grant interbank credits and carry out repo auctions.
"No sharp changes are being considered," Vagnorius said.
He added that any shift in currency policy would be carried out under the guidance of the IMF.
Vagnorius' said there may be a second stage in the currency's gradual shift to free convertability, when it may be linked to inflation.
He said the link would be to what future inflation was expected to be rather than what it had been in previous periods.
He said that if such a link was needed, it would not be put in place before summer 1997.
